\section[auctōritās, auctōritātis]{auctōritās, auctōritātis — authority, influence; backing}

\label{lesson:LA-C370-auctoritas}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to excuse, then the Latin for an excuse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: auctōritās, auctōritātis}
\textbf{auctōritās, auctōritātis} — \textquotedblleft{}authority, influence; backing\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Senex magnam auctōritātem in oppidō habet.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The old man has great influence in the town.}
\end{quote}

\emph{auctōritās, auctōritātis} f. A man's weight in public life, earned by age and deeds. English \emph{authority}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{auctōritās} is built on \emph{auctor} \textquotedblleft{}a backer, an originator\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which comes from \emph{augeō} \textquotedblleft{}to increase\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short). English \emph{authority} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{auctōritās, auctōritātis}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{auctōritās, auctōritātis}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{auctōritās, auctōritātis}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to excuse, then the Latin for an excuse, then say \emph{auctōritās, auctōritātis} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does auctōritās, auctōritātis mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Authority, influence; backing\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dignitās, dignitātis]{dignitās, dignitātis — worth, rank, dignity}

\label{lesson:LA-C370-dignitas}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for an excuse, then the Latin for authority.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dignitās, dignitātis}
\textbf{dignitās, dignitātis} — \textquotedblleft{}worth, rank, dignity\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Dignitātem suam semper servāvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He always kept his dignity.}
\end{quote}

\emph{dignitās, dignitātis} f., built on \emph{dignus}, worthy. A Roman's \emph{dignitās} is his rank and good name. English \emph{dignity}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dignitās} is built on \emph{dignus} \textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), with the ending \emph{-tās} that makes a quality. English \emph{dignity} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for an excuse, then the Latin for authority, then say \emph{dignitās, dignitātis} again
\end{itemize}

\section[gravitās, gravitātis]{gravitās, gravitātis — weight; seriousness}

\label{lesson:LA-C370-gravitas}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for authority, then the Latin for worth.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: gravitās, gravitātis}
\textbf{gravitās, gravitātis} — \textquotedblleft{}weight; seriousness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Cum gravitāte et sine īrā locūtus est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He spoke seriously and without anger.}
\end{quote}

\emph{gravitās, gravitātis} f., from \emph{gravis}, heavy. A Roman virtue: the seriousness of a man who weighs his words. English \emph{gravity}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gravitās} is built on \emph{gravis} \textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), whose cousins include Sanskrit \emph{guru} \textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{gravity} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for authority, then the Latin for worth, then say \emph{gravitās, gravitātis} again

\section[levitās, levitātis]{levitās, levitātis — lightness; fickleness}

\label{lesson:LA-C370-levitas}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for worth, then the Latin for weight.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: levitās, levitātis}
\textbf{levitās, levitātis} — \textquotedblleft{}lightness; fickleness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Levitātem eius omnēs reprehendunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Everyone blames his fickleness.}
\end{quote}

\emph{levitās, levitātis} f., from \emph{levis}, light: the opposite of \emph{gravitās}. English \emph{levity}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{levitās} is built on \emph{levis} \textquotedblleft{}light\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short): lightness of weight, then of character. English \emph{levity} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[temeritās, temeritātis]{temeritās, temeritātis — rashness, recklessness}

\label{lesson:LA-C370-temeritas}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for weight, then the Latin for lightness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: temeritās, temeritātis}
\textbf{temeritās, temeritātis} — \textquotedblleft{}rashness, recklessness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Temeritās iuvenis eum in perīculum dūxit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The young man's rashness led him into danger.}
\end{quote}

\emph{temeritās, temeritātis} f.: acting blindly, without a plan. English \emph{temerity}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{temeritās} is built on the adverb \emph{temerē} \textquotedblleft{}blindly, at random\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short). English \emph{temerity} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
